title: Local quantization under a smooth change of coordinates and real frames
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field] and the symbol estimates and oscillatory-integral normalization of [def-sfb-symbol-pseudodifferential-operators]. Let $U,V\subset\mathbf R^m$ be open, $m\geq1$, let $\kappa:U\to V$ be a smooth diffeomorphism, and let $H_E:U\to\mathrm{GL}_p(\mathbf R)$ and $H_F:U\to\mathrm{GL}_q(\mathbf R)$ be smooth, where $p,q\geq0$. Let $a\in S^r(V\times\mathbf R^m;\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(\mathbf C^p,\mathbf C^q))$, $r\in\mathbf Z$, and $\chi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$ be real. On compactly supported smooth inputs define $$L f(x)=\chi(x)H_F(x)\left[\operatorname{Op}(a)\left((H_E^{-1}\psi f)\circ\kappa^{-1}\right)\right](\kappa(x)).$$ Transport distributions by duality with test densities, including the absolute Jacobian. There exist $q\in S^r(U\times\mathbf R^m)$ compactly supported in $x$, a real $\mu\in C_c^\infty(U)$ equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}\chi\cup\operatorname{supp}\psi$, and a smooth compactly supported kernel $K$ on $U\times U$ such that $$L=\operatorname{Op}(q)\mu+R_K$$ on all distributions, and $$q(x,\xi)-\chi(x)\psi(x)H_F(x)a\bigl(\kappa(x),D\kappa(x)^{-T}\xi\bigr)H_E(x)^{-1}\in S^{r-1}.$$ All spatially supported symbols and kernels may be extended by zero to $\mathbf R^m$. The same assertion holds for the real parts of the quantizations; then the leading expression is replaced by its average under $q(x,\xi)\mapsto\overline{q(x,-\xi)}$.

source.place: WANTED locally: Part I §3.B, (3.4)–(3.5) and Proposition 3.7, printed pp.12–13. Global quantization before Proposition 3.6: change of coordinates and real bundle frames modulo one lower order. Agent-supplied local formulation. Supplemental course read online: https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf, §3, (3.3)–(3.6), 3.12–3.15, printed pp.6–12; coordinate-change and amplitude reduction details are supplied by the agent, not asserted to be proved in those notes.

proof.text: Put $J(y)=|\det D\kappa(y)|$. Apply the cited change-of-variables formula entrywise to the regularized integral, with the old input variable $z=\kappa(y)$. The kernel of $L$ is the tested cutoff limit with phase $(\kappa(x)-\kappa(y))\cdot\eta$ and amplitude $$d(x,y,\eta)=\chi(x)H_F(x)a(\kappa(x),\eta)H_E(y)^{-1}\psi(y)J(y).$$ This calculation includes the density Jacobian, and holds for the bilinear transpose as well. In old coordinates $X=\kappa(x),Y=\kappa(y)$ the spatially compact amplitude before the input Jacobian is $\chi(\kappa^{-1}X)H_F(\kappa^{-1}X)a(X,\eta)H_E(\kappa^{-1}Y)^{-1}\psi(\kappa^{-1}Y)$. It satisfies the cited amplitude estimates by the product and chain rules on the two compact supports. Amplitude reduction makes its operator and transpose continuous smooth-to-compact-smooth maps. Pullback, frame multiplication and the test-density Jacobian preserve this continuity: each derivative through order $k$ on a fixed compact is a finite sum of bounded smooth coefficients times input derivatives through order $k$ on its compact image. Thus $L$ on all distributions is the transpose of this test operator, exactly with the convention in its statement.

source.place: Local kernel and input-density change of variables; agent argument supplementing the online Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6) and 3.12–3.14.

proof.text: Near the diagonal, where the segment from $y$ to $x$ stays in $U$, put $$B(x,y)=\int_0^1D\kappa(y+t(x-y))\,dt.$$ The fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\kappa(x)-\kappa(y)=B(x,y)(x-y)$ and $B(x,x)=D\kappa(x)$. Smoothness and invertibility persist on an open neighborhood $W$ of the diagonal; shrink $W$ to these segment neighborhoods. Let $C_0=\operatorname{supp}\chi\times\operatorname{supp}\psi$. Its intersection with the diagonal is compact. Choose a relatively compact open neighborhood of that intersection whose closure lies in $W$, and a smooth real $\theta$ compactly supported in $W$ equal to one near that intersection. The cited smooth separating cutoff on $\mathbf R^{2m}$ supplies this function, using the compact intersection and the closed complement of the relatively compact neighborhood as the two closed sets. Split $d=\theta d+(1-\theta)d$. The second amplitude, expressed in old coordinates as in step 1 with the extra factor $1-\theta(\kappa^{-1}X,\kappa^{-1}Y)$, vanishes near the diagonal. The cited off-diagonal assertion gives a smooth compact kernel there. Its kernel in $U$ is obtained by composing with $(\kappa,\kappa)$ and multiplying by $J(y)$; it remains smooth with compact support in $U\times U$. Denote it by $K_0$.

source.place: Near-diagonal linearization and the separated smooth kernel; agent argument supplementing the online Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6) and 3.12–3.14.

proof.text: For $b=\theta d$ on $W$, the frequency-substitution lemma applies: its compact spatial support lies in $W$, its derivatives have the symbol bounds, and $D_y[B(x,y)(x-y)]=-D\kappa(y)$ is invertible. The near-diagonal kernel therefore has phase $(x-y)\cdot\xi$ and amplitude $$c(x,y,\xi)=\theta(x,y)\chi(x)\psi(y)H_F(x)a(\kappa(x),B(x,y)^{-T}\xi)H_E(y)^{-1}\frac{J(y)}{|\det B(x,y)|}.$$ This is an amplitude of order $r$ compactly supported inside $U\times U$. Indeed $B^{-T}$ and its derivatives are bounded on that support and $1+|B^{-T}\xi|$ is bounded above and below by positive multiples of $1+|\xi|$. Every spatial derivative hitting the frequency argument introduces one factor linear in $\xi$ and one additional frequency derivative of $a$; their orders cancel. Each explicit frequency derivative lowers the order by one. Products with the smooth compact spatial factors preserve these bounds. Extension by zero is smooth since the spatial support lies compactly inside $W$. The frequency lemma justifies the changed cutoff; ordinary finite-cutoff substitution alone would not do so.

source.place: Parameter-dependent frequency substitution; agent argument supplementing the online Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6) and 3.12–3.14.

proof.text: Apply amplitude reduction to $c$, within the prescribed open coordinate domain $U$. Write $$A_c=\operatorname{Op}(b_0)\mu_0+R_{K_1},\qquad b_0-c(x,x,\xi)\in S^{r-1}.$$ Here $b_0$ is compactly supported in $x$, $K_1$ is smooth compactly supported in $U\times U$, and $\mu_0=1$ near both spatial projections of $\operatorname{supp}c$. On the diagonal $B(x,x)=D\kappa(x)$, so $J(x)/|\det B(x,x)|=1$. Also $\theta(x,x)\chi(x)\psi(x)=\chi(x)\psi(x)$. Consequently $$c(x,x,\xi)=e(x,\xi):=\chi(x)\psi(x)H_F(x)a(\kappa(x),D\kappa(x)^{-T}\xi)H_E(x)^{-1}.$$ This proves the required leading expression before the cutoff adjustment.

source.place: Amplitude reduction and cancellation of the diagonal Jacobians; agent argument supplementing the online Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6) and 3.12–3.14.

proof.text: Let $X$ be the compact first spatial projection of $\operatorname{supp}c$. By the separating cutoff choose a real $\lambda\in C_c^\infty(U)$ equal to one near $X$ with support contained in the open set where $\mu_0=1$. Such a compactly contained neighborhood exists since $\mu_0$ is identically one near $X$. Since $A_c$ is supported in $X$ in its output variable, multiplication by $\lambda$ gives $$A_c=\operatorname{Op}(b)\mu_0+R_{\lambda K_1},\qquad b=\lambda b_0.$$ The support of $e$ in $x$ lies in $X$, so $b-e=\lambda(b_0-e)\in S^{r-1}$. Choose real $\mu\in C_c^\infty(U)$ equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}b\cup\operatorname{supp}\chi\cup\operatorname{supp}\psi$, again by the separating cutoff. The amplitude $b(x,\xi)(\mu_0(y)-\mu(y))$ vanishes near the diagonal: both cutoffs equal one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}b$. Its spatial support is compact. Its kernel $K_2$ is smooth and compactly supported by the off-diagonal amplitude assertion. Therefore $$L=\operatorname{Op}(b)\mu+R_K,\qquad K=K_0+\lambda K_1+K_2.$$ Rename $b$ as the statement's symbol $q$. All symbols and kernels have support compactly inside the indicated coordinate domains, so their zero extensions are smooth. Empty supports or a zero bundle rank give the zero amplitude and the same construction, with $b=K=0$ if $L=0$.

source.place: Cutoff enlargement without changing the principal symbol; agent argument supplementing the online Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6) and 3.12–3.14.

proof.text: Every kernel identity above was obtained as a tested cutoff limit, with continuous compactly supported smooth transposes supplied by amplitude reduction. Equality of kernels gives equality of their transposes on each smooth test density, and hence, for every distribution $u$ and test $\phi$, $(Lu)(\phi)=u(L^t\phi)=u((\operatorname{Op}(q)\mu+R_K)^t\phi)$. This proves the identity on all distributions, not only smooth inputs. For the real assertion the cited amplitude conjugation rule gives $a^\natural(X,\eta)=\overline{a(X,-\eta)}$. All spatial cutoffs, $B,J,H_E,H_F$ are real, so the transformed diagonal expression becomes $(e(x,\xi)+\overline{e(x,-\xi)})/2$. Replace the output symbol by $(q(x,\xi)+\overline{q(x,-\xi)})/2$ and the kernel by its real part. This averaging preserves the order $r-1$ remainder and every compact support, and gives precisely the real distributional action.

source.place: Distributional identity and the real conjugation involution; agent argument supplementing the online Demailly course §3, (3.3)–(3.6) and 3.12–3.14.
